result: ACEofBASEs is a web-based tool for base editing sgRNA design built on CCTop that identifies target sites, ranks sgRNAs based on editing window and dinucleotide context, and predicts off-targets.
evaluation: Claims C4, C24, C33-C38, and C88-C92 collectively describe the development and functionality of ACEofBASEs. The tool's architecture, features, and methodology are clearly documented with appropriate citations to the underlying CCTop tool and descriptions of its novel base editing-specific features.

result: Cytosine base editors ancBE4max and evoBE4max achieve high editing efficiencies (>93%) at the oca2 locus in medaka, substantially outperforming BE4-Gam (~29%), with evoBE4max showing reduced editing at AC dinucleotide contexts.
evaluation: Claims C25-C26, C39-C47 are supported by Sanger sequencing data (Figure 2e-f, Supplementary file 1) showing quantified editing efficiencies and phenotypic observations. The dinucleotide context preference for evoBE4max is confirmed both in vivo and by citation to in vitro studies (C44, Arbab et al., 2020).

result: ABE8e achieves high adenine base editing efficiencies in both medaka (up to 100%) and zebrafish (up to 95%) at oca2 loci, with pooled sgRNA injections increasing phenotypic penetrance but also aberrant phenotypes.
evaluation: Claims C48-C51, C119-C121 are directly supported by experimental data including Sanger sequencing quantification (Figure 2e-g, Supplementary file 2) and phenotypic scoring (Figure 2d, h-j). The correlation between editing efficiency and phenotype is demonstrated in both species.

result: Amplicon-seq analysis reveals high on-target editing efficiencies with editor-specific indel frequencies ranging from 2.1% (BE4-Gam) to 19.9% (ancBE4max), with deletions occurring predominantly at the Cas9 nickase site.
evaluation: Claims C52-C56 are supported by Amplicon-seq data (Figure 3, Supplementary file 4) showing quantified indel frequencies and deletion patterns. The comparison to Sanger sequencing (C53) validates the consistency of the two methods.

result: The editing efficiencies achieved in this study exceed those previously reported for cytosine and adenine base editing in fish, particularly for ABE8e compared to ABE7.10.
evaluation: Claims C57-C58 are supported by direct comparison of the current study's data to cited previous studies (Rosello et al., 2021b; Zhang et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2020; Qin et al., 2018). The quantitative improvements are documented in the experimental results.

result: ABE8e editing of transgenic GFP in medaka hearts achieves near-quantitative efficiency (97.0% ± 4.4%) with complete loss of fluorescence, demonstrating high editing activity even when delivered to single blastomeres.
evaluation: Claims C122-C125 are supported by fluorescence imaging, Sanger sequencing (Figure 4e-f, Supplementary file 2), and Amplicon-seq data (Figure 4g) showing high conversion efficiencies (85.9% ± 15.3%) with moderate indel rates (15.8% ± 17.5%).

result: Base editing of tnnt2a with evoBE4max creates a medaka 'silent heart' phenotype with high efficiency (85.9% ± 23.5%), which differs from zebrafish sih mutants and is faithfully reproduced in F1 homozygous mutants.
evaluation: Claims C126-C133 are supported by phenotypic observations, Sanger and Illumina sequencing data (Figure 5, Supplementary file 1), and F1 validation (Figure 5f'). The comparison to zebrafish phenotypes (C129) is appropriately cited (Sehnert et al., 2002).

result: Average C-to-T editing efficiencies of 38-88% were observed across tnnt2c and s1pr2 loci in F0.
evaluation: Claim C134 is directly supported by editing efficiency data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and Supplementary file 1.

result: ABE8e editing of the kcnh6a voltage sensor domain (R512G) achieves high efficiency (91.7% ± 9.5%) and results in non-contractile ventricles with ventricular collapse and aneurysm-like structures.
evaluation: Claims C135-C140 are supported by phenotypic observations (Figure 6b-c), genotyping data (Figure 6d), Amplicon-seq (Figure 6f), and high-resolution imaging (Figure 6g). The functional importance is corroborated by citation to electrophysiological studies (Zhang et al., 2004).

result: Single amino acid substitution in the ERG voltage sensor domain (R512G) produces a non-contractile ventricle phenotype comparable to null mutants, demonstrating base editing's capability to interrogate structure-function relationships.
evaluation: Claims C60-C62 are supported by experimental data showing the phenotype (Figure 6) and comparison to published zebrafish null mutants (Hoshijima et al., 2016). The novel morphological findings (C61) represent a previously unreported aspect of ERG function.

result: Base editing efficiently introduces missense mutations in four CHD candidate genes (dapk3, ube2b, usp44, ptpn11) with editing efficiencies of 54-100%, all resulting in cardiovascular phenotypes in F0.
evaluation: Claims C63-C64, C67-C68, C141-C143, C145-C146 are supported by editing efficiency data (Figure 7, Supplementary file 3), phenotypic observations (Figure 7d), and citations to human genetic studies (Homsy et al., 2015; Zaidi et al., 2013). The cardiovascular specificity is documented in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

result: Amplicon-seq data for ube2b experiments revealed slightly lower rates of intended edits (46.6% ± 11.9%) compared to Sanger sequencing, with low indel rates (4.9% ± 4.3%).
evaluation: Claim C144 is directly supported by Amplicon-seq data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

result: High-resolution imaging reveals specific cardiac morphological defects in usp44-E68K editants (abnormal AV channel, dysmorphic chambers) and ptpn11-G503E editants (small ventricle, linear atrium).
evaluation: Claims C147-C148 are directly supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 7f-g with corresponding editing efficiencies.

result: F1 analysis of dapk3 and usp44 mutants confirms F0 phenotypes, reveals bystander edit effects, and demonstrates incomplete penetrance for usp44-E68K, validating F0 base editing as an efficient screening approach.
evaluation: Claims C149-C152, C74 are supported by F1 genotype-phenotype correlation data (Figure 7h-i, Figure 7—figure supplements 6-7). The comparison between F0 and F1 generations validates the predictive value of F0 screening.

result: The study provides first functional evidence linking specific missense mutations in dapk3 (P193L/P204L), ube2b (R8Q), usp44 (E71/E68), and ptpn11 (G503E) to cardiac development, validating their association with human CHD.
evaluation: Claims C65-C66, C69-C73, C75-C76 are supported by experimental phenotypic data and appropriate citations to prior biochemical studies (Chang et al., 2010), genetic associations (Zaidi et al., 2013; Homsy et al., 2015), and functional studies (Fuchs et al., 2012; Stegmeier et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2012; Bonetti et al., 2014).

result: Comparison of Sanger and Illumina sequencing shows Sanger overestimates editing frequency and underdetects indels, but when overall modification is near 100%, moderate indels do not impact phenotypic conclusions.
evaluation: Claims C98-C102 are supported by direct comparison of the two methods on identical samples, with quantified differences documented. The inference about method choice (C99, C102) is reasonable based on the data and knowledge of sequencing limitations.

result: In vivo findings confirm in vitro dinucleotide context preferences for CBEs (TC>CC>AC>GC), with amelioration in ancBE4max and evoBE4max, while ABE8e shows no dinucleotide preference.
evaluation: Claims C103-C104 are supported by experimental data (Figure 8b-b') and appropriate citations to in vitro studies (Arbab et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2021; Komor et al., 2016; Richter et al., 2020). The in vivo confirmation of in vitro characteristics strengthens the findings.

result: Computational analysis reveals that CBEs and ABEs can model 5,896 human pathogenic CDS SNVs in medaka and zebrafish combined, with 1,951 modelable without bystander mutations, representing ~30% of ClinVar variants.
evaluation: Claims C77-C79, C105-C106 are supported by computational analysis of ClinVar data (Figure 8c) with appropriate citations to base editing papers (Gaudelli et al., 2017; Komor et al., 2016) and genome papers (Howe et al., 2013; Kasahara et al., 2007).

result: Expanded PAM editors (xCas9, SpRY) and evolved deaminases are projected to expand variant validation possibilities to cover up to 95% of pathogenic ClinVar transition mutations.
evaluation: Claims C80-C82 are projections based on citations to papers describing expanded PAM editors (Anzalone et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2018; Walton et al., 2020) and evolved deaminases (Chen et al., 2021; Koblan et al., 2021; Kurt et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2021). While the citations support the potential, the actual performance in fish has not been demonstrated in this study.

result: High editing efficiencies (close to homozygosity) in F0 embryos enable direct linking of specific mutations to phenotypes, overcoming bottlenecks in genome engineering for reliable somatic interrogation of DNA variants.
evaluation: Claims C27-C32, C59, C85-C86 are summary statements supported by the collective experimental data throughout the study showing high editing efficiencies, clear phenotypes in F0, and validation in F1. The conclusions about applicability are reasonable inferences from the demonstrated results.

result: The high precision and efficiency demonstrated suggest future applications including parallel editing of multiple sites and regulatory genome interrogation, with potential to improve personalized clinical care.
evaluation: Claims C83, C87 are speculative statements about future applications. While C84 is supported by citation to a recent study (Cheng et al., 2021), the broader claims about future impact (C83, C87) are not directly supported by data in this study and represent speculation about potential applications.

result: The study employed specific experimental protocols including sgRNA design parameters, injection concentrations for medaka (150 ng/µl editor, 30 ng/µl sgRNA) and zebrafish (360 pg editor, 40 pg sgRNA), with reduced concentrations for F1 experiments.
evaluation: Claims C93-C97 describe the experimental methods used in the study. These are straightforward methodological descriptions that are appropriately documented in the Materials and Methods section.
